evidence.source: 漢字構形資料庫, Academia Sinica
evidence.field: 字形演變; oracle bone and bronze form records
evidence.text: The database lists an oracle-bone example (合集19050) and a bronze example (集成02836). Its analysis identifies 天 and 元 with the human head: 天 depicts a front-facing person with the head emphasized, whose mark was later reduced to a horizontal stroke; it connects the head sense to ‘sky above’ by semantic extension.
evidence.title: 漢字「天」：字形演變

evidence.source: 考古資料數位典藏創新計畫, Academia Sinica
evidence.text: The account describes 天 as built on 大, a frontal standing human figure, with the upper mark indicating the head and later simplified to a horizontal stroke. It interprets the composite as ‘head/top of head’ and cites 說文’s 顛 gloss. This supports a human-figure graphic analysis; it is an institutional explanatory article, not a direct reading of a dated inscription.
evidence.title: 甲骨文 中與「天」相關的字

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: This reference likewise analyzes the graph as a standing human with emphasized head, and reports head-related use in oracle-bone inscription 合集20975 (弗疾朕天, interpreted as the king’s head) and personal-name use. It gives 天邑商 alongside 大邑商 as a Shang capital designation; it reports bronze uses for 天帝/天命 and 天子, and Warring States bamboo-slip examples of 天命 and 天下. The page supplies artifact or text identifiers, but not calendar dates for each example.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：天

evidence.source: 陳家寧, 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.field: section II, 天與大是同源字, lines 114–129
evidence.text: The author surveys oracle-bone and bronze shapes as 大-like human figures with the head marked, cites 王國維’s head/top analysis, and compares 天邑商 examples in 合集36535 and 36542 with 大邑商 in 合集36482 and 36530. The article argues that 天 and 大 were interchangeable or closely related in Shang-Zhou usage, while also acknowledging uncertainty over their exact graphic/lexical relationship. This cautions against treating every Shang 天 as unambiguously ‘sky/heaven’.
evidence.title: 陳家寧：說“大”、“太”和“天”的關係

evidence.source: Cho Yong Jun, KCI journal record and abstract
evidence.text: The 2024 study reports Shang oracle-bone 天 uses involving human heads and ritual recipients, and says 天 could interchange with 大 in the 天邑商 / 大邑商 expressions. It also cautions that surviving Shang materials do not establish a clear paired ‘earth/earth god’ versus ‘heaven/heaven god’ conceptual opposition. This is a modern interpretation of the corpus, not an inscription transcription.
evidence.title: Consideration of ‘Earth(土)’ and ‘Heaven(天)’ in the Oracle Bone Inscriptions of the Shang Dynasty

evidence.source: 陳家寧, 復旦大學出土文獻與古文字研究中心
evidence.field: section II, examples from oracle-bone and bronze corpora, lines 117–127
evidence.text: The article quotes Shang oracle-bone contexts 天邑商 (合集36535, 36542) and 大邑商 (合集36482, 36530), plus the bronze inscription on 何尊 reading 大邑商. It cites an older annotation that 天 in one oracle-bone phrase has the sense ‘great’ and concludes that 天 and 大 can be used interchangeably in Shang-Zhou material. These attestations support an early ‘great’/name-element use, but do not by themselves prove that the word 天 originated with that meaning.
evidence.title: 陳家寧：說“大”、“太”和“天”的關係

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.text: The entry distinguishes head-related oracle-bone usage (合集20975) from Shang 天邑商 / 大邑商 expressions, later bronze 天命 and 天子 examples, and Warring States bamboo-slip 天命 and 天下. This offers a plausible broad development from a head/top association to celestial and sovereign senses, but the page does not establish a dated, unbroken semantic chain for every step.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：天

evidence.source: 許慎, 說文解字, online text and 段玉裁 commentary
evidence.text: The Eastern Han dictionary entry reads 顚也。至高無上，从一、大, glossing 天 with 顛 and analyzing it as 一 plus 大. 段玉裁 explains 顛 as the top of a person and treats the ‘highest’ sense as extending to a general high position. This is an important historical lexicographic interpretation, not independent proof that the graph’s earliest word meant 顛 rather than sky/heaven.
evidence.title: 說文解字「天」

evidence.source: 劉熙, 釋名, in 識典古籍 transcription
evidence.text: The text gives the Han-era sound gloss 天顯也，在上高顯也 (‘heaven is manifest/high and conspicuous above’) and records regional pronunciation descriptions. This is an early received lexicographic account of the celestial word, not a secure etymology: the work uses sound glosses and should not be taken as proof of a prehistoric sound derivation.
evidence.title: 釋名·釋天

evidence.source: 章黃學術, Academia Sinica Institute of Linguistics
evidence.field: article excerpt on Han dialect variation, search result text
evidence.text: The inspected search result reproduces the 釋名 contrast: 豫司 etc. ‘天，顯也’ and 青徐 ‘天，坦也’, explicitly describing tongue-body versus tongue-tip pronunciations. This supports early dialectal pronunciation variation as reported by a Han lexicographic source; the PDF itself opened without extractable text, so the search-result excerpt is the accessible text consulted.
evidence.title: 《說文》、《釋名》中所反映的漢代方言現象

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry
evidence.field: 字源 and 词源, lines 278–286
evidence.text: This entry presents a competing account: the original word meant ‘sky’, while the head-like old graph was an anthropomorphic representation and the 顛 association later encouraged an erroneous derivation from 顛/巔. It reports that a formerly common Old Chinese aspirated-stop reconstruction has been replaced in recent work by a voiceless resonant reconstruction, citing dialectal and transcription evidence, while acknowledging that deeper etymology remains unknown. This is a tertiary synthesis and conflicts with the head-first interpretation in the Academia Sinica and CUHK analyses.
evidence.title: 天 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry
evidence.field: 上古汉语 comparison table and phonology summary, lines 264–286
evidence.text: The entry reports Zhengzhang Shangfang’s (2003) Old Chinese reconstruction *qʰl'iːn for 天 and discusses a voiceless resonant initial in newer proposals. The provided local Baxter–Sagart table row for 天 is *l̥ˤi[n] with Middle Chinese then; it is a distinct reconstruction system, not a conflicting transcription to merge with Zhengzhang’s notation. The Baxter–Sagart PDF search result also displayed 天 tiān / then / *l̥ˤi[n], but opening that PDF failed, so no claim here relies on that inaccessible page.
evidence.title: 天 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

gaps: Earliest graph evidence is represented here by oracle-bone and bronze corpus identifiers, but the inspected sources do not supply absolute dates for each cited 天 token. The approximate Shang dating range for those individual records was not independently established in the inspected material.

The Shang semantic evidence is contested: head-related tokens and 天/大 interchange are reported, but some scholars treat 天 as an early graph/word for ‘sky’; the available sources do not establish a single certain earliest spoken sense or a fully proven semantic chain from ‘head/top’ to ‘sky/heaven’.
No source inspected here demonstrates corruption of 天; the reduction of the head mark to a horizontal stroke is presented as graphic simplification, not textual corruption.

No phonetic component is proposed for 天. The visible 一 and 大 are treated in Shuowen as graphic elements, with 大 representing the human figure and the upper mark associated by paleographers with the head; neither is evidenced here as a sound component.

The supplied local Unihan row is kMandarin tiān for 天, but the mandated official Unicode character-specific record was inaccessible. It is therefore not used as externally verified evidence; no component reading is applicable.

The supplied local Baxter–Sagart row for 天 is *l̥ˤi[n] (MC then; also a western-dialect MC xen row). The upstream PDF was inaccessible, and no relevant component row exists because no phonetic component is being asserted. Zhengzhang *qʰl'iːn is reported by the inspected Wiktionary summary under a different reconstruction system; these notations should not be merged.

The inspected material supports sky/heaven, divine or sovereign uses, and Shang head-related and 天/大-related uses, but it does not provide a dated sequence for all later meanings such as ‘god’, ‘celestial’, or calendrical/time senses.
No glyph image was visually inspected in this research; form statements are attributed to the inspected character databases and scholarly discussions.

The inspected sources do not independently establish absolute dates for each cited oracle-bone or bronze token; artifact identifiers and script labels are available, but no precise dated sequence was verified here.

The earliest attested graph and earliest spoken sense remain distinct questions. Head-related oracle-bone usage is reported by CUHK and Academia Sinica, while sky-first analysis appears in the dossier’s tertiary source; available evidence does not establish a single certain semantic chronology or a complete head/top-to-sky chain.
The Fudan discussion supports interchange between 天 and 大 in Shang-Zhou usage but does not by itself show that 天’s spoken word originated with a ‘great’ meaning.
No inspected source reports graphic corruption. The documented mark-to-horizontal-stroke change is described as simplification.
No phonetic component is proposed: 一 and 大 are discussed as graphic elements in historical analyses, and no sound-component role is supported here.

The local Baxter–Sagart row provided for 天 is *l̥ˤi[n], with MC then and a western-dialect MC xen entry under the same OC notation; no component row applies. The official upstream PDF was not rechecked in this invocation, so the local dataset is not external evidence.
The official Unicode GetUnihanData record for U+5929 failed to open. The dossier-provided local Unihan row kMandarin=tiān is not represented here as externally verified evidence.

The Commons original SVG link was visible on the inspected file description page, but opening that direct link failed in the web tool. The page itself records CC0 and the Xiaoxuetang provenance; the glyph has not been visually inspected in this research.
The image correction is established by the inspected Commons description, but the SVG bytes/image could not be opened in this web session, so its visible strokes were not independently inspected.

Academia Sinica’s head-marked analysis is editorial interpretation. It supports phrasing 大 as the graphic basis for the person and the upper mark as emphasized head, but does not resolve whether the earliest spoken sense was head/top or sky/heaven.
Official Unihan GetUnihanData for U+5929 remained inaccessible; local reading rows were not used as external evidence.

The direct Commons SVG could not be opened by the web tool, so its rendered strokes were not visually inspected here. Its identity, Shang-style description, Xiaoxuetang exemplar reference, and CC0 status are established by the exact Commons description page.

The cited paleographic interpretation supports 大 as the graphic basis for the person and the upper mark as emphasized head, but does not establish a certain earliest spoken meaning or resolve the disputed head/top-to-sky semantic chronology.

The direct SVG could not be rendered by the web tool, so its visible strokes were not independently inspected in this research. The identity, source attribution, period label, and reuse notice come from its exact Commons description page.

The Shuowen seal-script image is a modern vector redraw, not a dated artifact image. Its selection illustrates a later script form, while the human-figure/head account is based on paleographic interpretations of earlier forms; the seal redraw alone cannot establish that interpretation or semantic chronology.

The inspected Academia Sinica account supports the wording that 大 is the graphic basis for the person and the upper mark emphasizes the head. It proposes a head-to-sky extension, but the dossier also records a competing sky-first analysis; the earliest spoken sense and semantic sequence remain unresolved.
